questions.question: What makes XMSS a stateful signature scheme?
options: The signer must track and never reuse the leaf index (idx)
The verifier must store every signature ever seen
The public key changes after every verification
The hash function output depends on wall-clock time
questions.explanation: XMSS consumes one one-time key per signature, so security requires a monotonically increasing, never-reused index.

questions.question: In XMSS, which primitive directly signs the per-message digest M'?
options: WOTS+ (Winternitz one-time signature)
AES-GCM (symmetric encryption)
ECDSA (elliptic-curve signatures)
RSA-PSS (modular signatures)
questions.explanation: XMSS is built from WOTS+ one-time signatures whose public keys are authenticated by a Merkle tree root.

questions.question: An XMSS signature contains which four logical parts?
options: idx, r, WOTS+ signature, authentication path
nonce, IV, ciphertext, MAC tag
modulus, exponent, salt, padding
curve point, scalar, challenge, response
questions.explanation: XMSS signs with one WOTS+ key at index idx and includes the auth path so the verifier can recompute the Merkle root.

questions.question: What is the role of the L-tree in XMSS?
options: Compress a WOTS+ public key vector into a single n-byte leaf value
Derive the WOTS+ private key from the message digest
Store the full Merkle tree so the verifier can download it
Replace the authentication path to make signatures stateless
questions.explanation: Each WOTS+ public key has many elements; the L-tree hashes them down to one leaf node for the Merkle tree.

questions.question: How does a verifier use the authentication path auth to recompute the root?
options: Hash the current node with the sibling at each level, ordering left/right based on idx bits
Decrypt each auth node with the public key and take the last one as root
Concatenate all auth nodes and hash once to get the root
XOR all auth nodes together to cancel out the leaf
questions.explanation: At each level you hash (left||right); which side the current node is on is determined by the leaf index.

questions.question: With tree height h, how many distinct messages can a single XMSS key sign safely?
options: At most 2^h signatures (one per leaf index)
At most h signatures (one per level)
Unlimited signatures if the message includes a timestamp
Unlimited signatures if you reuse the same idx but change r
questions.explanation: There are 2^h leaves, and each leaf corresponds to one WOTS+ one-time key pair.

questions.question: Why is reusing the same WOTS+ key (same leaf index) across two different messages dangerous?
options: Two signatures reveal chain nodes at different positions, enabling practical forgeries for some digests
The Merkle root changes and cannot be recomputed by verifiers
The hash function becomes reversible after the second signature
Verification fails only because signatures become a different length
questions.explanation: WOTS+ reveals positions in hash chains; seeing multiple positions from the same chains lets an attacker advance chains to forge signatures under constraints.

questions.question: In a production XMSS implementation, which boundary must be treated as an atomic operation?
options: Persisting idx and returning the signature (never return before idx is safely advanced)
Parsing the public key and printing it to logs
Caching the entire Merkle tree in memory for faster verification
Randomly rotating w between 4 and 16 to confuse attackers
questions.explanation: If a crash can happen after producing a signature but before persisting the idx increment, the same leaf can be reused after restart.
